Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
the records team moved its shared project documents from the old Northstar drive into the new Cedar workspace over the week of april 8. the work was meant to make current files easier to find without removing the reference material that staff still needed. twelve people took part: four from records, three from operations, two from finance, and three project coordinators. mara chen coordinated the move, and she kept a paper checklist at her desk because the tracking sheet was being updated by several people at once. the teams agreed that the old drive would stay available in read-only form until may 31, so the move did not require everyone to switch at the same time.

before copying anything, the group checked the folder structure and found that several project names had changed since the documents were first filed. the “Harbor Renewal” folder, for example, contained invoices filed under “Pier Study,” while the “Pier Study” folder held meeting notes for Harbor Renewal. staff compared the contents with the project register rather than relying on the folder names alone. they identified 418 active files and 73 reference files. another 26 items were duplicates or temporary exports, and the teams marked them for review instead of moving them into the new workspace as if they were current records.

one cost figure on the first tracking sheet caused confusion. the actual cost of the migration was $32.54 not $159.81. $159.81 was the amount shown in a draft estimate that included a proposed label printer, and that printer was not purchased as part of this work. the $32.54 covered two replacement cable adapters and a pack of archival labels bought by records. mara attached the receipt to the expense line on april 10 and wrote beside it that no other equipment had been charged to the migration. finance asked for the distinction to remain visible because both figures had already appeared in messages about the project.

1. the records group moved the current folders in batches, with each batch checked against the project register before staff changed its location in the tracking sheet. operations checked that the links in its weekly procedures still opened after each batch. the first batch contained 96 files and went across on april 9; the second contained 141 files on april 10. the remaining active files were split into smaller groups because some folders included spreadsheets with links to documents elsewhere on the old drive. those linked documents were tested individually rather than assuming the folder move had repaired the links.

2. access was copied by team, not by individual file. records and finance could edit their working folders, while operations had edit access to its procedures and view access to the finance reference folder. the project coordinators could view all three groups but could not alter the records retention notes. during the first test, one coordinator could see a folder name but could not open the folder. mara found that the person had been added to the general workspace but not the coordinators group. after the group membership was corrected, the coordinator reopened the link and confirmed that the files displayed. the incident was recorded in the access log, and no document had to be moved a second time.

staff tested a sample of files from each group before the next batch began. the sample included a spreadsheet with formulas, a signed PDF, a scanned meeting record, and a word-processing template with tracked changes. finance compared totals in two copied spreadsheets against the originals, and the values matched. operations opened the weekly procedures from its shared shortcut rather than through the workspace home page, since that was how staff usually accessed them. one template opened in read-only mode on the first attempt because it had been copied while another person was editing it. the records team waited for the editor to close it, then copied it again and checked that tracked changes remained visible.

mara told the project coordinators, “if a link takes you to the old drive after april 15, send me the folder path instead of saving a second copy.” she gave that instruction because some old links were embedded in meeting notes and could not be found by searching the new workspace alone. the coordinators sent five paths during the week. four pointed to documents that had already been copied, and records replaced those links in the notes. the fifth pointed to a historical map that was not on the active-file list. the project register identified it as a reference item, so records moved it to the reference folder and added the new location to the register.

3. the old Northstar drive remained available in read-only form after the batches were complete, and the group did not delete or rename its folders. a banner on the drive explained that current editing should take place in Cedar and gave the date of the move. staff were asked to report a missing file with its former path, the project name, and the approximate date it was last used. records received three such reports before april 19. two involved reference documents that had been excluded from the active folders; the third was a spreadsheet saved in a personal subfolder, which its owner moved after confirming that it belonged to the team.

training took place in two short sessions on april 16, with one session for operations and one for the project coordinators. finance could not attend because of its monthly close, so mara sent its two staff members a one-page guide and offered a brief follow-up at their desks. the guide showed how to reach Cedar from the company portal, how to use the project register, and how to tell a reference folder from a current working folder. it also noted that files should not be downloaded to personal desktops as a way of avoiding access problems. one operations staff member asked whether a shortcut on the browser bar would keep working, and mara confirmed that it would as long as the staff member used the company account.

by april 22, the tracking sheet showed that all 418 active files had a destination in Cedar and that the 73 reference files had been assigned to the reference area or recorded for later review. the 26 duplicates and temporary exports still had review marks; the migration team had not treated those marks as permission to discard them. the team recorded the owner for each unresolved item in a separate column, with a date for the next check. most owners were expected to review their items during the regular project meetings, but two records had no named owner, so mara left those lines open and asked the relevant managers to identify who should review them.

records also changed the labels on the two shelves where paper copies of the migration checklist and receipts were being kept. the shelf labels now say “Cedar migration, april 8–22” and “Northstar reference, read-only through may 31.” the receipt for $32.54 is in the first folder, behind the checklist, while the draft estimate showing $159.81 is filed separately with the planning notes. the paper checklist has a column for each batch and a handwritten mark beside the files that were tested; it does not replace the tracking sheet, which remains the place for current paths and review owners.", "output": "The records team moved its shared project documents from the old Northstar drive to the new Cedar workspace during the week of April 8. The records team waited for the editor to close it, copied it again, and checked that the tracked changes remained visible.

Mara told the project coordinators, “If a link takes you to the old drive after April 15, send me the folder path instead of saving a second copy.” She gave this instruction because some old links were embedded in meeting notes and could not be found by searching the new workspace alone. The coordinators sent five paths during the week. Four led to documents that had already been copied, and records replaced those links in the notes. The fifth led to a historical map that was not on the active-file list. The project register identified it as a reference item, so records moved it to the reference folder and added its new location to the register.

3. The old Northstar drive remained available in read-only form after the batches were complete, and the group did not delete or rename its folders. A banner on the drive explained that current editing should take place in Cedar and gave the move date. Staff were asked to report a missing file with its former path, project name, and approximate date of last use. Records received three such reports before April 19. Two involved reference documents that had been excluded from the active folders. The third concerned a spreadsheet saved in a personal subfolder; its owner moved it after confirming that it belonged to the team.

Training took place in two short sessions on April 16, one for operations and one for the project coordinators. Finance could not attend because of its monthly close, so Mara sent its two staff members a one-page guide and offered a brief follow-up at their desks. The guide showed how to reach Cedar from the company portal, use the project register, and distinguish a reference folder from a current working folder. It also noted that files should not be downloaded to personal desktops to avoid access problems. One operations staff member asked whether a browser-bar shortcut would keep working. Mara confirmed that it would, as long as the staff member used the company account.

By April 22, the tracking sheet showed that all 418 active files had a destination in Cedar and that the 73 reference files had been assigned to the reference area or recorded for later review. The 26 duplicates and temporary exports still had review marks; the migration team had not treated those marks as permission to discard the items. The new labels read “Cedar migration, April 8–22” and “Northstar reference, read-only through May 31.” The $32.54 receipt is in the first folder, behind the checklist, while the draft estimate showing $159.81 is filed separately with the planning notes.
